To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the retention of calcium was not significantly affected by prenatal vitamin-mineral supplements, the intake of dietary phosphorus was adequate for the majority of women, and the intake of dietary magnesium was inadequate.

The retention of calcium and phosphorus was adequate for both groups, but the retention of magnesium and iron was inadequate in both groups, and supplementation with iron and calcium salts did not improve the retention of either iron or calcium.

The retention of calcium, phosphorus, magnesium and iron by pregnant women consuming a self-selected diet supplemented with calcium, iron, and folic acid, was comparable to that observed in women consuming an unsupplemented diet of similar composition.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the adequacy of self-selected diets for pregnancy and with the effectiveness of prenatal vitamin-mineral supplementation.
the adequacy of the prenatal diet and not with the adequacy or the effectiveness of prenatal supplements.
the adequacy of the diets consumed by pregnant women.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the prenatal diet should provide adequate amounts of calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, and iron.
the retention of calcium, phosphorus, iron, and magnesium by pregnant women is dependent on the dietary intakes of these minerals.
the prenatal supplement is not a substitute for an adequate diet.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the retention of calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, and iron during pregnancy is related to the intake rather than the source of the minerals.

a good diet is essential for the proper development of the fetus, that the addition of a prenatal supplement does not guarantee that the diet will be adequate, and that the physician should be concerned about the quality as well as the quantity of the diet consumed by his pregnant patient.
the retention of calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, and iron was adequate for most of our subjects consuming diets with or without prenatal supplements.
The main takeaway from our work is that
prenatal supplements are not a panacea for poor dietary habits.
the prenatal supplement was well utilized and that the reliance on its effectiveness should not lessen the importance of a prenatal diet.
prenatal supplements are not always necessary, and that a well-rounded diet is often sufficient.
